kaigo-atomic-oral-details.heading: Oral care and dentures: keep the whole mouth clean
paragraphs: Oral care keeps teeth and the mouth clean to help prevent tooth decay, periodontal disease and bad breath. It also helps reduce oral bacteria, maintain saliva secretion and taste, and support appetite and eating. However, oral care alone does not completely prevent aspiration pneumonia or remove the need to assess swallowing.

Before starting, explain the care and check the mouth’s condition and support method. Observe gums, mucosa, remaining teeth and food residue while cleaning gently, a little at a time, without leaving areas uncleaned. With hemiplegia, also watch for food remaining on the affected side. Report the observed locations of bleeding, swelling or pain and the person’s complaints to healthcare professionals.

The source’s rinsing stage is not an instruction for everyone to perform unchanged. Individually check whether the person can rinse and spit and maintain posture, then choose a method according to oral/swallowing assessment and the plan. If difficult, do not force water into the mouth; check with the person responsible.

Stabilize posture and head position, remain alert to aspiration risk and avoid forcing the chin upward. Examples of meeting eye level from the front or supporting the head from behind prompt consideration of helper position and stability. Aspiration here means swallowed material or other substances entering the airway below the vocal cords; it differs from dysphagia, which means impaired swallowing function. A standing position alone does not prevent aspiration. Follow the person’s condition and a trained method.

Holding a toothbrush like a pencil is an example for controlling brushing force. Rather than rubbing hard, ask about sensations and adapt movements to teeth and gum condition. The grip alone does not determine safety.

Choose items such as foam oral swabs according to mouth condition and professional guidance. Do not treat them as always having the same cleaning effect as toothbrushes. Check product instructions, suitability and condition before and after use. Watch for problems such as detached foam; do not use an abnormal item, and tell the person responsible. Knowing an item’s name differs from using it safely.

This unit concerns removable dentures replacing missing teeth, also commonly called false teeth. Complete dentures replace all teeth; partial dentures replace some. There are upper and lower dentures. Dentures also collect food and dirt, so rinsing only the removed appliance does not complete all oral care.

Remove and clean dentures after meals or at other times according to the person’s plan. The source illustrates brushing off dirt and rinsing under running water. In practice, use brushes, water and any necessary cleansers appropriate to the denture material, following product instructions and dental-professional directions. After removal, also clean remaining teeth and oral mucosa using methods suited to each. Check dentures and the mouth separately.

The source illustrates storage using a clean container, water or cleanser. Consider risks such as drying-related cracks while checking material, dental-professional instructions and cleanser conditions. Do not independently dry dentures, disinfect them in boiling water or soak them in an unsuitable liquid. Report pain or wounds; care workers must not file dentures to repair them.

Textbook check example: if the person says ‘I washed my dentures, but not my remaining teeth yet,’ separately check what is complete and what remains. Respect what they can do and discuss necessary help. Actual care follows individual assessment, the plan and facility guidance.

kaigo-atomic-bath-sequence.heading: Connect checks during and after bathing
paragraphs: During bathing too, check condition, expression, skin and feelings. Look at the neck, armpits, groin and feet, as well as actual skin folds and areas where dirt remains easily. Unmarked areas in the source diagram are not areas that may be left unwashed.

Use accompaniment and equipment suited to condition during movement to prevent falls. Cover necessary areas with towels or similar items and respect feelings about exposure. The hemiplegia example places the care worker on the affected side, but actual position and method follow abilities, equipment and the plan.

Before pouring water, check temperature using an appropriate method and equipment, and ask about heat and discomfort. A worker touching water once does not establish continuing safety for the person. If they say it is hot, stop pouring and recheck temperature and condition. For altered sensation, do not rely on complaints alone: follow individual safe-checking methods.

The source illustrates gradually pouring water from the extremities toward the center and, with hemiplegia, starting on the unaffected side. This differs from deciding which side the worker stands on to support movement. Do not memorize a sequence and apply it to everyone. Check responses, facilities and the individual method as you proceed.

When washing the body, lather cleanser appropriately and avoid rubbing skin hard. Check dirt and skin folds and rinse cleanser away completely. Let the person do parts they can, and review methods if there is pain or discomfort.

In the bath-entry example, the person with hemiplegia enters from the unaffected side. Continue checking stable posture afterward and support the affected side, which may float, as needed. Getting into the bath does not complete assistance. Do not leave someone who needs support alone; continually check condition through expression and other cues.

Standing suddenly from the bath requires attention to unsteadiness from orthostatic hypotension. Help change posture slowly using support suited to the person and observe after they leave the bath. If abnormalities occur, stop bathing and follow facility procedures to seek assistance or contact healthcare professionals. Also check heat when pouring the final rinse.

For hair washing, wet the hair, use appropriately lathered shampoo and wash gently with finger pads. Do not scratch the scalp with nails. Keep water and shampoo out of the eyes, rinse away remaining shampoo and ask about discomfort.

After bathing, gently press with a dry towel instead of rubbing to remove moisture, carefully drying folds too. Arrange clothing to prevent chilling. Moisturize dry-prone skin according to the plan. Moisturizing differs from leaving water in folds. Report wounds or abnormalities rather than independently applying a new product and considering the matter resolved.

Use a hair dryer according to its instructions, checking temperature, distance and where air is directed. A diagram using the worker’s hand as a guide does not guarantee burn prevention. After drying, check condition and comfort and follow the individual plan for rest and fluids. Distinguish finished washing from completed post-bathing checks.

kaigo-atomic-partial-perineal-wash.heading: Partial baths and genital washing: cleanliness and privacy
paragraphs: A hand bath washes hands; a foot bath washes feet. Prepare a basin within reach or a container the feet can enter comfortably, with stable posture. Use a method suited to condition, whether seated or in bed, and let the person do parts they can.

Prepare suitably warm water and clean supplies. After washing, rinse away cleanser and gently remove moisture. Do not reuse water or equipment from another person or a dirty area unchanged for clean care. ‘Hand bath’ and ‘foot bath’ describe the area washed; they do not justify omitting hygiene checks.

The source explains that nails soften after partial bathing and become easier to cut. Softness alone, however, does not authorize nail cutting. Check nails, surrounding skin, illnesses and instructions, and consult healthcare professionals if abnormalities exist.

The genital area easily becomes soiled by excreta and sweat. Remaining dirty can contribute to odor or bacterial infection, so cleanliness matters. Do not diagnose infection from odor alone. Explain purpose and method, obtain consent, cover areas not needed and protect privacy. This area is temperature-sensitive; the source illustrates water warmed close to body temperature. Do not judge suitability from staff sensation or room temperature alone. Follow the person’s condition and established checking method.

The female-care example shows washing from the urethral area toward the anus. Do not move back and forth with the same surface; change surfaces or materials to avoid bringing contamination from the anal area toward the urethra. Beyond remembering ‘front to back,’ check where clean surfaces touch.

In male care, also check dirt and skin condition around the scrotum and in folds. Maintain cleanliness with a trained method based on consent and the individual plan. Report pain or skin abnormalities to healthcare professionals and do not forcefully pull skin or tissue.

After washing, gently pat dry and observe redness, pain or wounds. Report locations and the person’s complaints to healthcare professionals. Disposable gloves do not permit touching clean areas with contaminated surfaces. When moving from dirty to clean work, remove gloves appropriately, perform hand hygiene and change to necessary new gloves or materials.

Textbook check example: gloves alone do not maintain cleanliness if the surface used to wipe the anal area returns toward the urethra. Check washing direction separately from cleanliness of surfaces and supplies. Actual assistance follows assessment, the plan and facility procedures and training.

kaigo-atomic-icf.heading: Use ICF to consider functioning and environment together
paragraphs: The ICF, International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, is a framework for organizing functioning, disability and health to understand the person’s whole life. A diagnosis alone does not determine abilities. Consider health condition together with body functions and structures, activity and participation.

Body functions are how the body and mind work. Body structures are parts such as limbs and organs. Activity means performing tasks or actions, such as dressing or household work. Participation means involvement in life situations such as community gatherings or work. Do not treat these as interchangeable terms.

Environmental factors include housing, supporters, community resources and services, and people’s attitudes. An environment can facilitate or obstruct activity. Personal factors include age, experience, personality and values. People with the same diagnosis or age do not necessarily need identical support.

The diagram’s two-way arrows indicate relationships between components. Body functions affect activity, while environment and participation opportunities also influence what the person actually can do. Avoid a one-way understanding that illness makes all activity and participation uniformly impossible.

Textbook example: the person wants to join a book group, but the door is difficult to open when entering the room in a wheelchair. Record mobility, the environmental barrier of the door and the wish to participate separately. Ask about wishes and check accessible routes and necessary support with those involved. Do not treat the barrier solely as a problem with the person’s body.

The source illustrates how routes with suitable gradients can help mobility-equipment users access transport. A ramp’s presence alone does not establish safe use. Check actual slope and route, equipment, abilities and wishes when selecting support.

The personal-factor diagram includes sex and age, but these alone do not establish preferences or independence. Handle necessary information with a clear purpose and sharing scope and appropriate conditions such as consent. Actual support follows assessment and the individual plan.

kaigo-atomic-motor-disability.heading: Physical movement disability: check movement and understanding separately
paragraphs: Physical disability involving movement means difficulties in daily or social life arising from impaired limb, trunk or other movements due to illness or accidents. Causes include brain or spinal-cord injury, limb injury, deformities of bones, joints or spine, and joint contractures. Contracture makes a joint difficult to move. The label alone does not determine mobility-assistance methods.

Affected areas and severity vary individually. Difficulty moving fingers differs from understanding conversation. Cognitive or intellectual disabilities may coexist, but movement difficulty alone does not mean the person cannot understand. Check each ability and the support they want.

Canes, wheelchairs and prosthetic limbs serve different purposes. A prosthetic limb replaces part of a missing limb. Select equipment suited to health, abilities, life goals and environment, with necessary adjustment and use training. Possession alone does not establish safe use.

Textbook example: the person has difficulty moving a hand but answers questions clearly. Speak directly to them first and allow a response method and time that work. If family help is needed, check which parts the person wants help with. Do not exclude them from conversation because of hand movement alone.

Sharing affected areas, causes and current abilities separately helps identify necessary support. Actual assistance follows assessment, the individual plan and facility guidance. This explanation does not guarantee mastery of transfers or equipment-operation skills.

kaigo-atomic-hearing-disability.heading: Hearing disability: choose communication methods together
paragraphs: Hearing disability involves absent or reduced hearing that creates difficulties in daily life or social participation. The affected part of the pathway carrying sound through the ear to the brain, degree and onset vary. Age or hearing-aid presence alone does not establish audible sounds or understanding of words.

Hearing aids collect and amplify sound to support hearing. They do not completely restore previous hearing or separate every needed sound from background noise. Wearing one does not establish that an explanation was received. Ask about hearing and effective communication methods; check adjustment and use with the responsible professional.

Speak in as quiet a place as possible, from the front so expression and mouth movements are visible. Consider a known better-hearing ear too. Speak slowly and clearly without unnecessary volume. Rather than relying only on louder speech, check surrounding sounds and the person’s response.

Written communication conveys information through writing. Sign language conveys meaning through hand and finger movements, facial expressions and other features. Lip-reading uses mouth movements and related cues. Combine writing, sign language, lip-reading and hearing aids in useful ways for the person. Not everyone can use each method equally.

Choose methods after checking readable text, language, vision, experience with sign language or lip-reading, and wishes. Do not assume everyone with hearing difficulty signs or can understand everything by seeing the mouth. After communicating, check what was received in a way that places little burden on the person.

Textbook example: if guidance is not getting through to a hearing-aid user in a noisy room, first ask about the communication difficulty and discuss a quiet place or another method. Check together whether writing helps too. Follow individual assessment and the plan; workers must not change device settings alone.

kaigo-atomic-aphasia.heading: Aphasia: consider listening, speaking, reading and writing separately
paragraphs: Language and speech disorders broadly describe difficulties communicating through words due to problems in brain functions related to language, organs used for speech or other factors. Aphasia involves difficulty with previously acquired language functions following damage to language-related brain areas or similar causes. It can occur after a stroke. Understanding speech, speaking, reading comprehension and writing may be affected to different degrees. Check individual difficulties in each area.

Few spoken words alone do not establish lack of understanding, unwillingness to talk or loss of every cognitive function. Aphasia also differs from difficulty moving speech muscles alone. Language and speech-production problems can overlap, requiring appropriate professional assessment.

Use short, understandable words, communicate one point at a time and wait for replies. Do not interrupt intended meaning by correcting every small verbal mistake. Yes/no questions and choices can help when suited to the person, but do not interpret responses according to staff convenience.

Try pictures, photographs, gestures, choice boards, writing or assistive devices according to remaining abilities and wishes. Aphasia can also affect reading or writing: inability to speak does not guarantee ability to write. Share usable methods with professionals and the team.

Textbook example: after a stroke, spoken replies are few, but when shown pictures of two activities, the person selects the same picture. Record ‘few words’ separately from ‘a choice was observed in response to pictures,’ and check through a usable method whether that choice expresses their wish. One choice does not assess all language functions.

Allow time to check wishes. Do not invent them on the person’s behalf because staff cannot wait for words. Look for ways to enable participation, and tell the person responsible about observed responses and remaining uncertainties. Actual support follows assessment, the individual plan and professional guidance.

134.title: Oral care and dentures: keep the whole mouth clean
objectives: Clean the mouth and removed dentures using methods appropriate to each.
Explain conditions for posture, equipment and storage and changes requiring reporting.
134.context: Learn to check teeth, mucosa and dentures separately. Do not use source examples of posture or equipment as one procedure for everyone.
134.artCaption: The person and worker consult while looking at materials. The picture does not show mouth observation or denture cleaning itself.

135.title: Connect checks during and after bathing
objectives: Connect checks of condition, water and posture during bathing with checks afterward.
Distinguish the worker’s position from the side where water is first poured.
135.context: Learn checks from bathing through hair washing, drying and rest. Adapt procedures to responses and individual assistance methods.
135.artCaption: A worker prepares water, towels and other supplies beside a bed. The picture does not establish assistance inside a bath or a completed temperature check.

136.title: Partial baths and genital washing: cleanliness and privacy
objectives: Explain partial-bath scope and clean/dirty boundaries in genital washing.
Distinguish unconfirmed specific techniques from matters to observe or consult about.
136.context: This unit covers partial baths and genital cleanliness. Some specific male-washing techniques remain unverified; do not infer and perform them from pictures.
136.artCaption: A worker stands near a surface with clean supplies and a container for used items. The picture alone guarantees neither supply cleanliness nor an actual washing technique.

137.title: Use ICF to consider functioning and environment together
objectives: Distinguish body functions/structures, activity, participation and environmental factors.
Consider support using both personal goals and environmental barriers.
137.context: Organize relationships between the person and environment rather than judging life by diagnosis alone. Use the project-created book-group example to distinguish activity and participation.
137.artCaption: The person and worker check the route near a doorway step. This scene considers personal movement together with the environment.

138.title: Physical movement disability: check movement and understanding separately
objectives: Separate areas with movement difficulty from checks of understanding and wishes.
Explain the need for equipment selection, adjustment and use training.
138.context: Learn causes and individual differences in physical movement disability, focusing on directly checking responses and wishes.
138.artCaption: Workers explain using an anatomical model. The picture does not assess a particular person’s abilities or transfer-equipment fit.

139.title: Hearing disability: choose communication methods together
objectives: Ask which communication methods help and arrange a supportive listening environment.
Distinguish hearing-aid use from successful communication of an explanation.
139.context: Hearing and usable methods differ individually. Choose communication with the person rather than relying on volume alone.
139.artCaption: The person speaks while a worker listens and records. Do not infer hearing-aid use or hearing level from the picture.

140.title: Aphasia: consider listening, speaking, reading and writing separately
objectives: Distinguish four language areas and specifically record observed responses.
Choose personally suitable pictures, gestures or writing and check wishes.
140.context: Learn aphasia-related difficulties and support using remaining abilities. Choosing a picture alone does not assess all language functions.
140.artCaption: A worker shows pictures of drinks or food and waits for a response. Showing pictures alone does not confirm the person’s wishes.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-oral-details.prompt: Which approach to oral care is appropriate?
options: Treat all mouth checks as complete if the removed denture is clean.
Treat cleaning remaining teeth as unnecessary for denture users.
Use the denture-washing method unchanged on all oral mucosa.
Also check remaining teeth and mucosa and provide care appropriate to each.
rationales: Denture cleaning and checking inside the mouth are separate. Some areas remain unchecked.
Remaining teeth also need cleaning. A partial denture does not make this unnecessary.
Dentures and mucosa are different targets. The same equipment and method are not always suitable.
This separates completed from unchecked areas and considers care needed throughout the mouth.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-oral-details.reading: Textbook example: a partial denture has been removed and washed. The remaining teeth and oral mucosa have not yet been checked.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-sequence.prompt: What is an appropriate next response?
options: Exclude the person’s reaction from temperature checks because the worker already checked by hand.
Stop pouring and recheck the person’s condition and water temperature.
Treat the first check as evidence of safety until bathing ends.
After hearing the complaint, only checking whether hemiplegia is present is enough.
rationales: The worker’s sensation alone cannot determine suitability for the person.
This takes the complaint seriously and checks temperature and condition before continuing.
Temperature and condition need continuing checks. One check does not guarantee the entire course.
Hemiplegia is one piece of information, but it does not replace the complaint about heat or checking water.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-bath-sequence.reading: Textbook example: the worker checked the water by hand. When it was poured, the person said, ‘It is too hot.’

options: Gloves alone do not maintain cleanliness. Check direction and clean surfaces and materials.
With gloves, using the same surface in either direction remains clean.
Remembering a back-and-forth direction removes the need to check contamination of the surface used.
Hand hygiene can be omitted after removing gloves.
rationales: A direction that does not return contamination and a clean surface are necessary. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene or management of task boundaries.
Even with gloves, a contaminated surface can transfer dirt to another area.
Check both direction and the surface used to avoid bringing contamination toward the urethra.
Hand hygiene is needed after glove removal. Having worn gloves does not justify omission.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-partial-perinea.reading: Textbook example: during genital washing, a gloved worker is about to return toward the urethral area using the surface that wiped the anal area.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-icf.prompt: Which organization of information uses the ICF perspective?
options: Establish the reason for nonparticipation solely from the diagnosis.
Do not record the door in considering functioning because it is outside the person.
Distinguish mobility, the wish to participate and the door as a barrier, and check necessary support.
Once the environment is changed, checking wishes and movements is always unnecessary.
rationales: Diagnosis alone cannot explain relationships among actual activity, participation and environment.
Environmental factors relate to activity and participation. A difficult-to-open door matters too.
This distinguishes the person and environment while considering their interaction.
Environmental arrangements and checking wishes and abilities belong together; either alone is insufficient.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-icf.reading: Textbook example: the person wants to attend a book group. They use a wheelchair to approach the room, but the door is difficult to open.

options: Because hand movement is difficult, only ask family about wishes.
Speak directly to the person and check a workable response method and desired support.
Treat clear answers as evidence that every action is possible without assistance.
Omit individual movement and understanding checks if equipment is available.
rationales: Movement difficulty alone does not establish inability to understand or express wishes.
This separates movement and understanding while preserving participation in the checks.
A clear reply does not prove independence in every action.
Equipment presence alone does not establish safety or individual abilities.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-motor-disabilit.reading: Textbook example: the person has difficulty moving a hand but answers questions clearly. Without asking them, the worker plans to ask only family about wishes.

options: Record the guidance as received because the person uses a hearing aid.
Do not check room noise when a hearing aid is present.
Always switch exclusively to lip-reading without asking about experience when hearing is difficult.
Ask about communication difficulty and wishes, and discuss a quiet place or another usable method.
rationales: Wearing the device and understanding the guidance are separate matters.
Noise affects hearing and may not be fully removed by the aid.
Ease of lip-reading varies. Check experience and wishes.
This checks both environment and personally useful methods. Choose writing only after checking whether it works for the person too.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-hearing-disabil.reading: Textbook example: in a noisy room, guidance is not getting through to a hearing-aid user. The worker is considering only speaking louder.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-aphasia.prompt: How should this observation be handled?
options: Few words mean the response to pictures cannot be used at all in checking wishes.
Choosing the same picture completes assessment of listening, speaking, reading and writing.
Record verbal and picture responses separately and check wishes using a method suited to the person.
If speaking is difficult, assume the person can always answer in writing.
rationales: Look for ways to use remaining abilities. Few words alone do not make picture responses meaningless.
One observed choice does not assess every language aspect.
This accurately records what was observed and supports participation and checking wishes.
Aphasia can also affect writing and reading. Check the suitability of written communication individually.
weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-aphasia.reading: Textbook example: after a stroke, spoken replies are few, but when shown pictures of two activities, the person chooses the same picture.
